strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely novel and clean mechanism for power-law loss decay: softmax plus cross-entropy learning peaked distributions produces power-law vanishing loss/gradient (L ~ β^{-1}, gradient ~ β^{-2}), and gradient flow then inevitably yields L ~ τ^{-1/3}. This is independent of data structure, qualitatively distinct from prior 'static' and 'dynamic' scaling-law theories that attribute exponents to power-law data spectra or feature frequencies.

The core derivation is simple, transparent, and self-contained (Taylor expansion of the free energy plus time integration), giving it the flavor of a universality argument in statistical physics, which the authors use appropriately rather than overclaiming literal universality.

The empirical program is thorough and well matched to the theory: high/low temperature regimes are both derived and observed; SGD vs. Adam, learning-rate scans, initialization-scale scans, learning-rate schedules, and weight decay are all systematically tested; curve collapse under dynamic time τ is used as a sharp falsifiable prediction; a deeper residual-MLP toy model supports robustness beyond the single-layer case.

The LLM analysis on Pythia checkpoints is a thoughtful attempt to bridge toy model and practice: entropy-matching argument that next-token distributions lie in the low-temperature regime (β* ≈ 6.87 > c0 ≈ 4.55), fitted exponent α_τ ≈ 0.33 close to the predicted 1/3, collapse across model sizes when plotted against τ, and the logit-standard-deviation growth exponent ~1/3 as a mechanistic signature.

Limitations are honestly discussed (gradient noise, unsolved rotation regime, need for robustness proofs), and the implications for weight decay, learning rate scheduling, and optimizer design are concrete and plausible.
weaknesses: The aligned student ansatz is heuristic and only partially justified (small initialization, silent-alignment intuition); more importantly, the regime that the LLM evidence actually enters at late training — loss decaying via parameter rotation while logit std saturates (Figures 5c,d, 6c) — is outside the theory. Result 3 is explicitly only a 'heuristic explanation'. Since this rotation regime appears to dominate the later, arguably most relevant part of LLM training, the theoretical account of the very phenomenon the paper claims to explain is incomplete.

Attribution is not established: the theory shows softmax+cross-entropy is a *sufficient* mechanism for 1/3 scaling, but does not show it *dominates* over data-structure mechanisms in real LLMs. Both could coexist and produce similar exponents; the paper's claim that this is the mechanistic explanation for observed neural scaling goes beyond the evidence. The observed agreement of many exponents in the 0.28–0.34 range (Chinchilla's 0.28, Pythia fits) is consistent with, but not uniquely explained by, this mechanism; the reinterpretation of Chinchilla's 0.28 as an artifact of learning-rate schedules is plausible but not directly validated.

The Pythia fitting involves discretionary choices: L∞ is a free parameter, the points included in the power-law fit are selected because they 'visually' lie on a line, and only the last ~11 checkpoints per model are used — the early-training regime (arguably where loss is not yet low-temperature) is excluded, which weakens the claim that the whole training trajectory obeys the predicted scaling. Confidence intervals or model-comparison baselines (e.g., fitting against data-seen rather than τ, or alternative functional forms) would strengthen the case.

The toy model uses a random Gaussian teacher as the target, whereas the actual target in LLMs is a fixed, structured data distribution; the mapping from the teacher inverse temperature β* to real LLMs relies on an entropy-matching construction with i.i.d. Gaussian logits that the authors themselves note is rough and not directly comparable to actual logit statistics.

Some presentation issues: several key claims (e.g., why Adam follows gradient flow on average, why ceff is constant) are acknowledged as unexplained assumptions; Figure 6c's saturation interpretation requires the weight-decay analogy whose quantitative match is not verified; and statements like 'first theoretical study' are somewhat overreaching given related concurrent work (Liu et al., 2025b; Barkeshli et al., 2026) that the authors discuss but distinguish only qualitatively.

strengths: The core derivation (low-temperature free-energy expansion + gradient flow giving β ~ τ^{1/3} and L ~ τ^{-1/3}) is elegant, self-contained, and verifiable with only Taylor expansion and time integration; the statistical-mechanics framing (partition function, free energy, internal energy) is coherent and clearly presented in Appendices A.1–A.4.

The theory is validated within the toy model at multiple levels: static loss/gradient curves (Figure 3), high-temperature exponential regime (Figures 10–11, 17–18), learning-rate and initialization-scale sweeps, SGD vs. Adam, learning-rate schedules, and a deeper residual toy model (Section D.6). The high/low temperature regimes with a predicted boundary at c0 ≈ √(2 ln n) are a nice falsifiable structure.

Empirical evidence on Pythia checkpoints (loss collapsing across model sizes when plotted against dynamic time τ, fitted exponent α_τ ≈ 0.33, logit standard deviation growing with exponent ≈ 1/3 before saturating) is an inventive use of public checkpoints, and the logit-std observation (norm growth then rotation, mirroring the weight-decay toy experiments in Figure 5c,d) is genuinely interesting.

The limitations section is honest, and the authors are careful in places (e.g., acknowledging that the rotation-driven 1/3 regime is not theoretically explained, and that c_eff for Adam is an assumption justified only post hoc by theory–experiment agreement).
weaknesses: The bridge from toy model to LLMs — the paper's central claim — rests on plausibility arguments rather than proof or discriminating experiments. The claims that data structure 'does not change the Taylor expansion argument' and that transformer/embedding components 'may not matter' are explicitly 'not proved but supported' (Section 4). There is no experiment that isolates this mechanism in a real LLM against data-structure-based alternatives; the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis but not exclusive to it.

The LLM exponent fitting is vulnerable to selection bias: the authors fit only 'the last 11 points that are visually on one line' (Section D.7), discarding earlier checkpoints, and the distinguishing margin over Chinchilla's 0.28 is small. A power law near 1/3 in time is also predicted by several data-structure theories in relevant regimes, so the observed exponent match is weak discrimination, and no falsification test (e.g., training on controlled data with known spectral structure) is performed.

The aligned student ansatz — the load-bearing assumption for the entire solvable analysis — is motivated heuristically from weight visualizations (Figure 2) and small-initialization folklore. The rotation-driven regime (Result 3), which the LLM weight-decay analysis ultimately invokes, has only a hand-waved explanation ('power-law vanishing loss and gradients likely occur for all parameter directions'), so a substantial portion of the LLM-relevant phenomenology lies outside the theory.

The argument that next-token distributions are 'sufficiently peaked' relies on a crude reduction: an irreducible-loss-derived entropy upper bound (1.69 from Chinchilla) mapped to an equivalent i.i.d. Gaussian-logit system, giving β* ≥ 6.87 vs. c0 ≈ 4.55. This equivalence is acknowledged to be approximate, and the conclusion that 'LLMs operate in the low-temperature regime' is therefore fragile; the logit std of real LLMs is admitted to be non-Gaussian and not directly comparable.

Adam dynamics are approximated by gradient flow with a fitted constant c_eff, whose mechanistic justification is deferred to future work; several key results (e.g., optimal learning rate, Adam with weight decay) are thus described rather than derived, weakening the 'mechanistic explanation' framing.

The claim of being 'the first theoretical study' of softmax/cross-entropy-driven power laws and the repeated emphasis on 'universal' exponents overstate the evidence: universality is demonstrated only for one random teacher-student setup with specific architectural choices (RMSNorm-style initialization, one head), and related concurrent work (Liu et al. 2025b, Barkeshli et al.) is positioned dismissively without detailed comparison of predictions.

Some claims about practical implications (avoiding weight decay, new optimizers, token-hierarchy architectures escaping the low-temperature regime) are speculative and not supported by any experiment in the paper.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely distinct mechanism for power-law loss scaling — softmax plus cross-entropy on peaked distributions — that is independent of power-law structure in the data, complementing the dominant data-centric theories (Michaud et al., Bordelon et al., Bahri et al., etc.). This is a novel and interesting perspective.

The core derivation is clean and transparent: low-temperature expansion of the free energy (L ~ β^{-1}, gradient ~ β^{-2}) plus gradient flow yields β ~ τ^{1/3} and L ~ τ^{-1/3}. The statistical-mechanics framing (free energy, internal energy, universality) is well motivated and pedagogically effective.

Experimental support in the toy model is unusually thorough: temperature scans over three orders of magnitude, learning-rate scans for both Adam and SGD, dynamic-time collapse, initialization-scale scans, learning-rate schedules, weight decay, and a multi-layer residual extension (Section D.6). The high-temperature exponential regime is also derived and confirmed, delineating when power laws do and do not appear.

The LLM validation is thoughtful: using Pythia checkpoints, the paper shows (i) fitted exponents α_τ ≈ 0.33 across four model sizes with curve collapse under dynamic time τ, and (ii) logit standard deviation growth with exponent ~1/3 followed by saturation, mirroring the weight-decay toy model behavior. This goes beyond mere exponent fitting and tests intermediate predictions of the mechanism.

Reproducibility is good: code and notebooks are named concretely (exp-1.py, pythia-logit-i.ipynb, etc.), and hyperparameters are documented in detail. The limitations discussion is honest, explicitly acknowledging that the ansatz is unproven for misaligned students, that gradient noise is untreated, and that the rotation-driven 1/3 regime lacks analytic explanation.
weaknesses: The central analytic result rests on the aligned student ansatz, which is empirically motivated (Figure 2) but not proven, and the derivation is closed only under it. The case where the ansatz fails yet 1/3 scaling persists (Figure 5c-d, rotation-driven decay) receives only a heuristic explanation ('power-law vanishing gradients likely occur for all parameter directions'). The paper is candid about this, but it means the universality claim is not fully established even within the toy model.

The bridge from the teacher-student toy model to LLM training is indirect. The teacher's peaked distribution is a fixed object, whereas in LLM training the target next-token distribution is implicit in the data and the loss is over data, not a fixed teacher. The quantitative temperature argument (entropy ≤ 1.69 from Chinchilla's irreducible loss → equivalent i.i.d. Gaussian β* = 6.87 > c0) is a crude chain of estimates: it depends on treating Chinchilla's irreducible loss as an entropy upper bound and on replacing structured language logits with i.i.d. Gaussian logits whose c0 is analytic.

The LLM exponent evidence involves fitting flexibility: L_τ and c_τ are fitted constants, and the power-law region is selected as the 'last 11 points' that are 'visually on one line' (Section D.7). The gap between the fitted α_τ ≈ 0.33 and Chinchilla's 0.28 is small, and the explanation for the discrepancy (nonlinear data-size vs. dynamic-time relationship) is asserted rather than independently verified.

The theory is derived under gradient flow with negligible noise and constant c_eff. Real LLM training uses Adam with large learning rates, warmup, and decay; the paper argues empirically that small-LR Adam follows gradient flow and shows schedule agreement in the toy model (Section D.4), but why Equation (21) describes Adam at scale is explicitly left to future work (A.1). The claim that data properties beyond peakedness only affect coefficients is plausible but unproven, and the interplay with data-driven power-law mechanisms (both may coexist) is not disentangled empirically.

The fitted toy-model exponents (loss exponent 1.15 ± 0.04, gradient exponent 2.26) deviate noticeably from the ideal 1.0/2.0 even in controlled settings, and the power-law window requires β well below β*; how wide this intermediate regime is for realistic LLM temperatures is not quantified, leaving some tension in the 'universal exponent' narrative.

The claim to be 'the first theoretical study' showing softmax/cross-entropy can drive power laws is slightly strong given recent related arguments the authors themselves cite (Liu et al., 2025b; Barkeshli et al., 2026); the differentiation (explaining the small time exponent) is fair but should be stated more carefully.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely novel and clean mechanism for power-law loss decay: softmax + cross-entropy on peaked distributions produce power-law loss/gradients via a low-temperature expansion, independent of power-law structure in data. This is a distinct alternative to the prevailing data-centric theories of neural scaling laws and is framed attractively via the statistical-mechanics universality analogy (free energy, internal energy, partition function).

The core derivation (Sections 3, A.2-A.4) is simple, self-contained, and checkable: L ~ c2 β^-1, gradient ~ β^-2 under gradient flow gives β ~ τ^(1/3) and L ~ τ^(-1/3). The high-temperature regime is also worked out, correctly predicting exponential convergence for flat distributions, and these predictions are verified numerically (Figure 3, 9-11, 17-18).

Empirical validation is unusually thorough for a theory paper: the 1/3 scaling is shown under SGD and Adam, with learning-rate scans, learning-rate schedules, initialization-scale scans, weight decay, power-law data covariance, a deeper generalized toy model with residual layers, and MLP training on MNIST (fitted exponent 0.35). The collapse of loss curves when plotted against dynamic time τ is a nice, discriminating test.

The LLM experiments are informative and well-designed: using published Pythia and OLMo checkpoints, fitting L = c_τ/τ^α_τ + L_⟩τ, showing cross-model collapse in (L − L_⟩τ, τ) with fitted exponents 0.31-0.37, and comparing collapse quality of τ vs. t fits (R^2 = 0.98 vs 0.93). The logit-standard-deviation growth analysis (Figure 6d) connecting to the toy model's low-temperature signature is a clever diagnostic.

The limitations are discussed honestly and specifically (gradient noise, inability to explain the rotation-driven 1/3 regime, the heuristic nature of the entropy-based temperature boundary for LLMs), and code availability is promised with detailed reproducibility information in appendices.
weaknesses: The gap between the toy model and actual LLM training is substantial and only bridged heuristically. The theory assumes i.i.d. Gaussian inputs, i.i.d. Gaussian logits, a fixed teacher, and effectively one-layer dynamics; real LLMs have evolving hidden states, attention, embeddings, and multi-layer interactions. The paper's own analysis of weight-decay experiments shows that 1/3 scaling can arise via mechanisms (rotation) the aligned-student theory cannot explain, so the theoretical picture is incomplete even within the toy setting.

The argument that LLM next-token distributions are 'low temperature' relies on a rough construction: matching the entropy of language distributions with i.i.d. Gaussian logits using an upper bound on entropy (1.69 from Chinchilla's irreducible loss). This is an indirect proxy; the actual per-context next-token entropy is likely far below the bound, and logit standard deviations of real LLMs cannot be directly compared to c0 (as the authors concede). The conclusion that LLMs 'enter the low-temperature regime' is therefore weaker than presented.

The LLM evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, the proposed mechanism. Data-driven theories (power-law spectra, feature frequencies) also predict power-law loss decay with similar exponents, and the paper does not disentangle or rule out these alternative contributions; the claim that this architectural mechanism 'dominates' in LLMs is not directly tested (e.g., no intervention or ablation).

The 1/3 exponent itself is not very discriminative: fitted LLM exponents range 0.31-0.37, prior literature values (0.28, 0.30, 0.36) are similar, and the fitted loss exponent in the toy model (1.15 ± 0.04 vs theory 1) shows some tension. The selection of fitting windows (e.g., 'the last 11 points seem to be on one curve') involves post-hoc choices, and the free constant L_⟩τ absorbs model-dependent effects.

The reduction to a one-dimensional effective dynamic rests on the aligned student ansatz, whose justification is heuristic ('small initialization promotes rotation'), and the extension of gradient-flow dynamics to Adam is an assumption justified mainly by the agreement of experiments, with ceff treated as an empirical constant. The assumption ρ_ϵ2(0) > 0 needed for c2 ≠ 0 is plausible but unverified for real language data.

The novelty claim ('first theoretical study showing softmax and cross-entropy can be the key to power-law training') is stated strongly; the relationship to closely related concurrent lines (Barkeshli et al., Liu et al., superposition-based theories) deserves a more careful delineation of what is genuinely new beyond the specific exponent derivation.

strengths: The core theoretical mechanism is clean and well-derived: for softmax + cross-entropy learning peaked distributions, the low-temperature expansion gives L ~ β^{-1} and gradient ~ β^{-2}, which under gradient flow yields β ~ τ^{1/3} and L ~ τ^{-1/3}. The derivation requires only mild, clearly stated assumptions (peaked target distribution, non-zero density of energy-gap distribution at zero), making the 'universality' claim plausible.

The paper systematically tests the mechanism beyond the base setup: power-law structures in data (D.6), deeper residual architectures (D.7), and MNIST classification (D.8), all showing the same exponent. This is a genuine attempt to establish the robustness/universality of the result.

The 'dynamic time' τ analysis of LLM checkpoints is a nice methodological point: collapsing Pythia loss curves across model sizes with fitted exponents 0.31–0.37 and the R²=0.98 vs 0.93 comparison (τ vs t) provides quantitative, if indirect, support.

Limitations are discussed honestly (gradient noise, unexplained rotation-driven 1/3 scaling, heuristic nature of the Adam-as-gradient-flow assumption), and the writing/presentation of results (boxed results, clear figures) is generally good.
weaknesses: There is a substantial inferential gap between the toy model and the central claim about LLMs. The toy model is a teacher-student setup with i.i.d. Gaussian inputs and a frozen teacher; real LLM training involves co-evolving hidden states, data, and body parameters. The paper shows LLM behavior is 'consistent with' the mechanism but cannot demonstrate the mechanism dominates in LLMs; no interventional test on real LLMs (e.g., modifying output temperature, vocabulary size, or loss function and checking the predicted change in scaling) is provided.

The LLM evidence rests on 3-parameter fits (c_τ, α_τ, L_{\τ}) to ~11 checkpoint points, with L_{\τ} freely fitted per model. This leaves room for degeneracy and post-hoc selection (e.g., 'the last 11 points seem to be on one curve' is chosen visually; early points are excluded as a different regime without independent justification).

The theory-verification fits in Figure 3 show exponent 1.15±0.04 for loss vs β (theory predicts 1) and 2.26±0.01 for the gradient (theory predicts 2). These deviations, while modest, are glossed over rather than explained, weakening the claim of quantitative agreement.

The aligned student ansatz is justified heuristically (small initialization promotes alignment) and verified only via 2D projections of weight rows (Figures 2, 12), which is weak evidence. The extension to rotation-dominated regimes (Figure 5c,d) has no analytic support — acknowledged, but it means the theory does not cover a regime the authors themselves rely on for LLM interpretation (Pythia uses significant weight decay).

The claim to be 'the first theoretical study' of softmax/cross-entropy-driven scaling is overstated: the paper itself cites Liu et al. (2025b) and Barkeshli et al. (2026) arguing scaling without power-law data, and the t^{-1/3}-type exponent from gradient flows with vanishing gradients is a familiar mechanism pattern.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link in footnote 1 is empty in the manuscript, and while file names (exp-1.py, etc.) are given, a working artifact is not verifiable from the submission.

The reconciliation with prior empirical exponents (Kaplan 0.095, Chinchilla 0.28) is somewhat convenient — discrepancies are attributed to fitting choices, but no quantitative re-analysis is offered, and the paper does not clearly state what observational signature would falsify the proposed mechanism versus data-driven explanations.

strengths: The paper poses a clear and well-motivated question: can power-law loss decay arise from architectural components (softmax + cross-entropy) rather than power-law structure in the data? This is a genuinely interesting mechanistic hypothesis that complements the dominant data-centric explanations.

The core theoretical derivation is clean and transparent: the low-temperature expansion of the free energy (Section A.3) yields L ~ β^{-1} and gradient ~ β^{-2}, which under gradient flow gives β ~ τ^{1/3} and L ~ τ^{-1/3}. The derivation requires only Taylor expansion and time integration, and the paper is appropriately careful that the result holds in the intermediate regime only.

Theory and experiments are well connected in the toy model: Figures 3, 4, 7, and 8 show that measured loss and inverse temperature agree quantitatively with predictions, including the exponent of β growth (~0.38 vs theoretical 1/3), collapse under dynamic time τ, and the high-temperature exponential regime (Figures 10, 11, 17, 18).

The LLM experiments are a meaningful attempt at validation beyond toy settings: Pythia and OLMo checkpoints show fitted exponents 0.31–0.37 with curves collapsing across model sizes when plotted against dynamic time τ, and the R² comparison (0.98 for τ vs 0.93 for t) is a reasonable quantitative test of the claim that τ is the fundamental variable.

The paper demonstrates robustness across many extensions: power-law data structures (D.6), deeper residual architectures (D.7), MNIST classification (D.8), weight decay (D.5), and learning rate schedules (D.4), which supports the universality framing.

The limitations are discussed candidly (Section 6), including the unexplained rotation-driven 1/3 scaling under weight decay and the unanalyzed effects of gradient noise; this honesty strengthens confidence in what is and is not established.
weaknesses: The central claim that this mechanism is relevant to or dominates in LLMs is supported only by consistency, not necessity. The fitted 1/3 exponent in Pythia/OLMo could plausibly arise from other mechanisms (e.g., data-structure-driven scaling, or artifacts of the learning rate schedule used to define τ). The paper does not perform a control that would distinguish the softmax/peakedness mechanism from alternatives in real LLMs.

The argument that LLMs are in the low-temperature regime is heuristic: it maps real next-token distributions onto an equivalent i.i.d. Gaussian-logit ensemble by matching entropy (Figure 6a), and the key theoretical condition ρ_{Δε}(0) > 0 (non-zero density of zero energy gaps) is explicitly unverifiable for LLMs (Section A.3). This weakens the transfer of the toy-model exponent to actual LLMs.

The rotation-driven 1/3 scaling observed under weight decay (Figure 5c,d), which is arguably the regime most analogous to late-stage LLM training (logit std saturates while loss still scales as 1/3, Figure 6d), is not covered by the solvable theory; the explanation is only 'heuristic' (Section 3). Thus the theory-experiment link for the LLM-relevant regime is the weakest part of the chain.

Modeling Adam as gradient flow with a constant c_eff is a stated assumption rather than a derived result (Appendix A.1); the authors acknowledge the mechanistic justification 'requires future studies'. Since Adam is what is actually used in the toy and LLM experiments, this is a nontrivial gap.

The choice of L\τ in Equation (20) adds a free fitted constant per model, and fitted exponents vary (0.31–0.37 for Pythia; 0.30–0.36 for OLMo); the paper's argument that Chinchilla's 0.28 differs only due to a nonlinear dataset-size-to-τ mapping is plausible but not demonstrated quantitatively.

Some bold claims are under-supported: 'the first theoretical study showing that softmax and cross-entropy can be the key to power-law training behaviors' is difficult to verify, and 'universal' requires careful qualification (which the paper does provide, but the abstract's phrasing overreaches).
The footnote 'Code available at' appears incomplete (no URL is visible), which hinders reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed experimental descriptions and code file names.

Generality beyond the one-layer teacher-student setting is only empirically argued; the theory has not been extended to multi-layer networks, so the claimed independence of 'many other details' rests on the assumption that logits approximately follow gradient flow.
